title: A Window Held by a Threshold

scenes.tts: Close one eye of a young mouse for a few days, and its visual cortex answers that eye much less. Do the same to an adult, and far less happens. We can ask why in the mouse, because its genes can be changed. So what opens the window? Is it simply age?
scenes.visual: Young and adult cortex responses to each eye; the young cortex shifts to the open eye, the adult barely; a question mark over age.
scenes.narration: Close one eye of a young mouse for a few days, and its visual cortex answers that eye much less. Do the same to an adult, and far less happens. We can ask why in the mouse, because its genes can be changed. So what opens the window? Is it simply age?

scenes.tts: A knockout mouse lacks a working copy of one gene. Mice make GABA with two enzymes, and one of them, G A D sixty-five, supplies GABA when neurons fire hard. A knockout without it shows no shift after an eye is closed, even at the normal age. Its neurons still respond to vision. What failed was the change.
scenes.visual: Two enzymes make GABA; GAD65 is crossed out; the knockout cortex bars stay put after the eye closes.

scenes.tts: Now add diazepam. It makes the GABA receptor respond more strongly to GABA, but it cannot open the receptor alone. Think of a smoke detector that needs a minimum charge before it sounds. The knockout's battery is low, and diazepam tops it up. Given during deprivation, it restores the shift.
scenes.visual: A receptor whose response grows with diazepam; an inhibition meter below a threshold rises over it and the window lamp turns on.

scenes.tts: A normal mouse has its window in a few weeks of youth. Knockouts kept their capacity for a critical period into adulthood. There, diazepam triggered the window whenever it was given. In normal young mice, diazepam before the usual opening started the window early. It also ended early.
scenes.visual: An age axis with three rows: the normal window, the knockout opened by diazepam late, the normal mouse opened and closed early.

scenes.tts: If the window simply faded, nothing could open it again. Several experiments suggest it is held shut by brakes. A dense lattice of matrix condenses around many parvalbumin cells. Myelin signals act through the Nogo receptor, and a protein called Lynx one damps nicotinic receptors. In adult rodents, taking away brakes kept plasticity or restored it.
scenes.visual: A fading window versus three brakes pressing it shut; each brake lifted in turn lets the window open.

scenes.tts: Inhibition has to reach a threshold to start the window, and brakes are added to end it. Boosting inhibition does not shift the cortex by itself, but it lets the cortex respond to deprivation. In mice and rats, genes, drugs and experience can move both steps. These results show mechanism, not treatment for people. So keep this rule: a critical period is a state of a circuit, not an age.
scenes.visual: One plot: inhibition crosses a threshold, the window opens, brakes end it; both ends slide when genes, drugs or experience act.
